questions.q: What three things does the action + artifact + framework pattern require a resume bullet to name?
options: What you did, what you produced that a reviewer could ask to see, and what standard or tool you used
Your job title, your start date, and your manager's name
A list of every software tool you have ever opened
The company's revenue and headcount
questions.explain: The lesson defines the pattern as action (what you did), artifact (what you produced), and framework (the standard or tool applied).

questions.q: Which of these is the strongest example of the pattern, per the lesson?
options: "Wrote and ran 12 SQL data quality checks against a 6-table customer domain, combined into one UNION ALL failures report"
"Worked on data quality for the customer domain"
"Helped with some SQL stuff"
"Responsible for data"
questions.explain: This 'after' version names a real number, a real artifact (the failures report), and a real technique (UNION ALL) — exactly the pattern the lesson teaches.

questions.q: According to the lesson's suggested resume structure, where should capstone deliverables typically go for someone at this career stage?
options: Prominently, near the top, often above general work Experience
Left off the resume entirely since they are training exercises
Only in the Education section
Mixed into the Skills section with no separate listing
questions.explain: The lesson's one-page structure places capstone/project deliverables early, since for career changers or those building a path-specific resume, projects often carry the most relevant proof of work.

questions.q: What mistake does the lesson warn against regarding describing your own role in a decision?
options: Blurring whether you decided a policy versus implemented one someone else approved
Mentioning the word 'policy' at all
Using too many bullet points per deliverable
Listing your email address on the resume
questions.explain: The lesson ties this directly to the owner/steward distinction from earlier in the path — be precise about which one you actually were.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say inconsistent numbers across your resume and portfolio are a problem?
options: Because a careful reviewer will notice the mismatch immediately and question your credibility
Because resumes and portfolios are not allowed to both contain numbers
Because applicant tracking systems automatically reject resumes with any numbers
Because numbers are never appropriate on a governance resume
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly calls out mismatched numbers between documents as the first thing a careful reviewer notices.
